definitions.definition: Atrocities means offences as specified under Section 3 of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, committed by a person who is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe against a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, encompassing acts of violence, humiliation, exploitation, and social or economic oppression perpetrated on the basis of caste identity.
definitions.plain_english: Atrocities refer to serious wrongs and cruel acts committed by people from upper or other castes against members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. These include acts of physical violence, sexual harassment, social humiliation, forced labour, and denial of basic rights based solely on the victim's caste identity. The law treats these acts as especially serious crimes because they are rooted in caste-based discrimination and oppression.
real_world_examples: An upper-caste landlord in Uttar Pradesh forcibly occupies agricultural land allotted to a Dalit farmer by the state government and physically prevents the Dalit farmer from cultivating it.
In a village in Rajasthan, dominant caste members force a Dalit person to carry a dead animal carcass on their shoulders through the public street as a form of collective punishment and humiliation.
A contractor in Tamil Nadu compels Scheduled Caste workers to manually clean sewage pits without protective equipment, constituting manual scavenging under the Act.
In Maharashtra, a group of dominant caste men parade a Scheduled Tribe woman naked through the village after a dispute, causing extreme public humiliation.
A politician in Bihar intimidates Dalit voters before elections, warning them not to vote for a particular candidate or face social and economic boycott of the entire Dalit community.
A local leader in Madhya Pradesh insults a Dalit Panchayat Chairperson in a public meeting by repeatedly using their caste name in an abusive manner, intending to humiliate them before others.
what_it_covers: Physical acts of violence such as assault, parading naked, garlands with footwear, or forcible tonsuring committed against an SC/ST member by a non-SC/ST person.
Economic and land-related offences such as wrongful occupation or dispossession of land allotted to an SC/ST member, or interference with forest rights.
Forced and degrading labour including compelling an SC/ST person to do begar, manual scavenging, or carry human or animal carcasses.
Sexual offences including non-consensual touching of a sexual nature and sexual gestures or words directed at an SC/ST woman with knowledge of her caste identity.
Social and political coercion such as forcing an SC/ST person not to vote, not to file a nomination, or imposing social or economic boycott after elections.
Acts of public humiliation including abusing an SC/ST person by caste name, intentional insult with intent to humiliate, or defiling objects sacred to SC/ST communities.
what_it_excludes: Offences committed by a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe against another SC/ST member, as the perpetrator must be a non-SC/ST person for the Act to apply.
General criminal acts such as theft, fraud, or assault between persons that have no caste-based motivation and are not directed at the victim on the basis of their SC/ST identity.
Acts committed against a person who does not belong to a notified Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, even if the act is otherwise identical in nature to a listed offence.
Compulsory service for public purposes lawfully imposed by the Government, which is explicitly excluded from the definition of forced or bonded labour under Section 3.
Private disputes or civil wrongs between non-SC/ST and SC/ST persons that arise from personal, commercial, or contractual grievances without any caste-based dimension.

definitions.plain_english: An 'atrocity' refers to any serious crime or wrong committed against a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe community that is specifically listed and made punishable under Section 3 of this Act. These are acts intended to humiliate, harm, exploit, or oppress people from these communities because of their caste or tribal identity. The law uses this term to distinguish such targeted offences from ordinary crimes under the Indian Penal Code.
real_world_examples: A Dalit man in a village in Rajasthan is forcibly made to parade naked through the streets by upper-caste community members to publicly humiliate him — this constitutes an atrocity under Section 3(1) of the Act.

A group of dominant-caste individuals in Tamil Nadu dump human excreta in front of the house of a Scheduled Caste family to demean and intimidate them — this is an atrocity punishable under Section 3.

An upper-caste landlord in Bihar forces a Scheduled Tribe agricultural worker to perform begar (forced labour without wages) under threat of physical harm — this qualifies as an atrocity under the Act.

A Scheduled Caste woman in Uttar Pradesh is sexually assaulted by a non-SC/ST individual who exploits her caste-based social vulnerability — this is an atrocity attracting special prosecution under the Act.
Members of a dominant community in Maharashtra prevent a Scheduled Caste candidate from filing nomination papers for a local Gram Panchayat election — this constitutes an atrocity under Section 3.
A person in Madhya Pradesh deliberately contaminates the drinking water source exclusively used by a Scheduled Tribe hamlet — this act of defilement is an atrocity under Section 3 of the Act.
what_it_covers: Any offence listed under Section 3 of the Act committed against a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, such as forced consumption of noxious substances, humiliation in public view, or forcible dispossession of land.
Acts of sexual exploitation or assault targeting Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe individuals where the offender is a non-SC/ST person, as enumerated under Section 3.
Wrongful occupation or cultivation of land belonging to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe person carried out by a person not belonging to such communities, as covered under Section 3.
Forced labour or begar imposed on members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes by non-SC/ST individuals, constituting an atrocity under Section 3.
Deliberate insults or intimidation intended to humiliate a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member in a place within public view, as penalised under Section 3.
what_it_excludes: Offences committed by a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe against another member of the same or another SC/ST community, as Section 3 targets non-SC/ST perpetrators committing crimes against SC/ST victims.

General criminal offences under the Indian Penal Code (such as theft or ordinary assault) that do not fall within the specific list of offences enumerated under Section 3 of this Act, even if the victim happens to be from an SC/ST community.

Civil disputes involving Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe individuals — such as property inheritance disagreements or contractual disputes — that do not involve the specific penal conduct described in Section 3.
Acts of economic boycott or social boycott alone, unless they amount to a specific offence listed under Section 3 and are therefore separately governed under distinct provisions of the Act.

Atrocities committed by public servants in their official capacity where such conduct is covered exclusively under other laws and does not constitute one of the specific enumerated offences under Section 3.

definitions.definition: "Begar" refers to a form of forced or unpaid labour extracted from a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe against their will, without remuneration or consent, typically as a result of their caste identity. As used in Section 3 of the Act, compelling a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe to do begar or other forms of forced or bonded labour — other than any compulsory service for public purposes imposed by the Government — constitutes a punishable atrocity.
definitions.plain_english: Begar means forcing someone to work without pay or against their will simply because they belong to a lower caste. It is a deeply exploitative practice where Dalit or Adivasi individuals are compelled to provide labour — such as farm work, domestic service, or carrying loads — by upper-caste individuals or landlords without any wages. This practice is rooted in caste-based oppression and is treated as a serious criminal offence under this law.
real_world_examples: An upper-caste landlord in rural Rajasthan forces a Dalit agricultural labourer to work his fields during harvest season without paying any wages, threatening social ostracism or physical harm if the labourer refuses.

A dominant-caste village head in Uttar Pradesh compels Scheduled Caste women to cook and clean at his household during wedding celebrations without any payment, under threat of eviction from their rented land.

A brick kiln owner in Bihar forces bonded Dalit workers — who had taken a small advance loan — to continue working indefinitely without wages, effectively trapping them in debt bondage that constitutes begar.

A landlord in Tamil Nadu coerces a Scheduled Tribe family to carry his goods and personal luggage between villages without compensation, invoking their traditional caste-based obligation to serve him.

In a village in Madhya Pradesh, Scheduled Caste men are forced by the dominant community to clean and maintain the community well without pay, under threat of being denied access to common village resources.
A sugarcane farmer in Maharashtra compels Dalit migrant workers to work extra unpaid hours beyond their contracted duty under threat of withholding their meagre contracted wages.
what_it_covers: Forcing a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member to perform agricultural or domestic labour without payment under threat, intimidation, or social coercion.
Debt bondage arrangements where a Dalit worker is compelled to work indefinitely without wages in purported repayment of an advance or loan given by an upper-caste employer.

Traditional caste-based obligations where Scheduled Caste individuals are coerced to provide labour services — such as carrying loads, tending livestock, or manual tasks — to dominant-caste households without remuneration.
Compelling Scheduled Tribe members to perform unpaid community labour exclusively because of their tribal identity, under duress or threat of harm or economic boycott.
what_it_excludes: Compulsory service for public purposes lawfully imposed by the Government, such as statutory obligations for disaster relief, public health emergencies, or civic duties applicable to all citizens equally.
Voluntary consensual labour arrangements where a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member freely agrees to work and is fairly compensated, with no element of coercion or caste-based compulsion.

Court-ordered community service or state-mandated public works programmes that apply universally and are not targeted specifically at Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe individuals on the basis of their caste identity.
Manual scavenging, which — though similarly coercive and caste-based — is separately and distinctly penalised under a different sub-clause of Section 3 of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Code" means the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974).
definitions.plain_english: The word 'Code' in this law is a shorthand reference to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which is the main procedural law governing how criminal cases are investigated, tried, and decided in India. Whenever the SC/ST Act mentions the 'Code', it means that the rules and procedures laid down in that central law will apply. This ensures that investigations, arrests, bail, trials, and appeals under the SC/ST Act follow the standard criminal procedure framework of India.
real_world_examples: When a police officer registers an FIR for an atrocity committed against a Dalit person in a village in Rajasthan, the investigation procedures — such as recording statements, conducting searches, and arresting the accused — are carried out following the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

Under Section 18A of the SC/ST Act, which references the Code, an accused person charged with an atrocity offence cannot seek anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the SC/ST Act restricts this provision.

When a Special Court in Tamil Nadu conducts a trial for an offence under the SC/ST Act, it follows the trial procedure prescribed in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, including examination of witnesses, cross-examination, and recording of evidence.

A magistrate in Maharashtra, while taking cognizance of an atrocity offence reported by a tribal victim, applies the provisions of the Code regarding summoning of the accused and framing of charges as mandated by the procedural framework referred to in the SC/ST Act.

If an accused convicted under the SC/ST Act wishes to appeal the judgment, the appeal is filed and processed according to the appellate procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as adopted by reference in the SC/ST Act.
what_it_covers: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Act No. 2 of 1974) in its entirety, including all its chapters, sections, and schedules as applicable to criminal proceedings.

Every person in the group can then be held equally responsible for the crime, even if only one person physically committed the act.

After losing a panchayat proceeding, a group of five upper-caste men together attack and assault the Dalit family. The court presumes all five acted with common intention due to the prior dispute.

Following a dispute over water channel rights in rural Maharashtra, a group of OBC farmers collectively raid a Scheduled Tribe farmer's land, destroy his crops, and beat him. Since the offence follows a pre-existing dispute, all members of the raiding group are presumed to share common intention under Section 8.

In Uttar Pradesh, after a Dalit man files a complaint against a zamindar, a group of the zamindar's associates jointly burn the Dalit man's house at night. The joint act combined with prior enmity leads to a presumption of common intention among all accused.

A group of men from a dominant community in Tamil Nadu, after a dispute over a wedding procession route through their street, collectively assault Scheduled Caste residents during the procession. All participants are held jointly liable under the presumption of common intention arising from the pre-existing social dispute.

In Madhya Pradesh, three persons together forcibly tonsure a Scheduled Caste woman and parade her through the village following a dispute over grazing rights. The coordinated nature of the act and the preceding dispute trigger the presumption of common intention against all three accused.

definitions.definition: Consent, as used in the Act, means voluntary and uncoerced agreement by a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe to an act done against or upon their person; consent obtained by putting the person, or any other person in whom the person is interested, in fear of death or of hurt does not constitute valid consent. An act done without the person's consent, against the person's will, or under coerced consent amounts to an aggravated offence under Section 3.
definitions.plain_english: Consent means that a person freely and willingly agreed to something being done to them, without any force, threat, or fear. If someone agrees only because they were threatened with death or serious harm to themselves or someone they care about, that agreement does not count as real consent. Under this law, doing something to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe person without their genuine consent, or by tricking them through fear, is treated as a serious criminal offence.
real_world_examples: A Dalit woman in a village is touched in a sexual manner by a dominant-caste man; she does not agree to it and the act is done without her consent, making it an offence under Section 3(1)(w)(i) of the SC/ST Act.

A dominant-caste landlord threatens to harm a Dalit farmer's family unless the farmer agrees to sign over his land; even if the farmer signs, such consent obtained under fear of hurt is invalid, and the land transfer constitutes an offence under Section 3.

A Scheduled Tribe woman is pressured into a devadasi dedication ceremony after being told her family will be socially boycotted and harmed if she refuses; her apparent agreement is not valid consent under the Act.
A Dalit labourer is forced to carry a human carcass after being threatened with violence; any apparent compliance is not voluntary consent, and the act of compulsion is punishable under the Act.

A Dalit voter is intimidated into voting for a particular candidate by threats of economic harm to his household; his compliance does not constitute consent, and the offender is liable under Section 3.

what_it_excludes: Genuine, freely given, uncoerced agreement by the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe person, which would negate the commission of the specific offence requiring non-consent as an element.

definitions.definition: Criminal conspiracy, as applied under this Act by virtue of Section 6, adopts the meaning and provisions of Chapter VA of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), which defines it as an agreement between two or more persons to do or cause to be done an illegal act, or an act which is not illegal by illegal means, in furtherance of the purposes of this Act. Where the illegal act agreed upon constitutes an atrocity or offence under this Act, the conspiracy itself becomes punishable under the Act's enhanced provisions.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal conspiracy means when two or more people secretly agree and plan together to commit a crime — in this context, a crime targeting Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe members. The agreement itself is the crime, even if the planned act was never carried out. So if a group of upper-caste villagers sit together and plan to attack a Dalit family or burn their crops, all of them can be held responsible from the moment they agreed on the plan.
real_world_examples: A group of dominant-caste landowners in a village in Rajasthan meet and agree to collectively assault a Dalit farmer who filed a land dispute claim, planning the attack in advance — all participants are liable for criminal conspiracy under the SC/ST Act even if one person actually carries out the assault.

Several upper-caste individuals in a Tamil Nadu town plan and coordinate to force a Scheduled Tribe family to vacate their forest land by threatening violence and destroying their crops — their prior agreement to execute this plan constitutes criminal conspiracy under this Act.

In a Maharashtra village, a group of people conspire to organize a social boycott of an entire Scheduled Caste community by secretly dividing roles — some to threaten shopkeepers, others to block water access — making all conspirators equally punishable.

Two or more persons in Uttar Pradesh agree to falsely implicate a Scheduled Caste government employee in a fabricated criminal case to humiliate him and force his removal from a dominant-caste neighbourhood, and take preparatory steps toward that goal — their agreement itself constitutes criminal conspiracy under this Act.

A group of contractors in Bihar agree among themselves to prevent Scheduled Tribe labourers from accessing worksites and to extract begar (forced labour) from them, planning and dividing responsibilities in advance — each member of this agreement is guilty of criminal conspiracy.

In Andhra Pradesh, members of a dominant community plan together to desecrate a Scheduled Caste community's place of worship and coordinate the roles of each participant — the planning meeting itself establishes criminal conspiracy regardless of whether desecration ultimately occurs.
what_it_covers: An agreement between two or more persons to commit any offence or atrocity under the SC/ST Act, even if the agreed act was not ultimately carried out.
Pre-planned coordination among a group of upper-caste individuals to humiliate, assault, dispossess, or socially boycott members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.

Situations where different persons agree to play distinct roles in committing an atrocity — one to threaten, one to execute violence, one to serve as a lookout — making all equally liable as conspirators.
Any meeting of minds between two or more persons to use illegal means (e.g., intimidation, false cases, forced displacement) against SC/ST individuals or communities, even if preparatory.
Conspiracy to commit acts that themselves attract punishment under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, including economic boycott, sexual exploitation, or forced labour against SC/ST persons.
what_it_excludes: A single individual independently planning and executing an offence without any prior agreement with another person — criminal conspiracy requires a minimum of two parties.
Mere knowledge or suspicion of another person's criminal intent without any active agreement or participation in the conspiracy.
Accidental or coincidental joint action by multiple persons who had no prior agreement or shared criminal plan — spontaneous individual acts do not constitute conspiracy.
Agreements to do acts that are entirely lawful and do not involve any illegal element or illegal means, even if the outcome disadvantages SC/ST persons.
Civil disputes or collective petitions against SC/ST individuals pursued through lawful legal channels, which do not involve agreement to commit an illegal act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Applying the criminal conspiracy provision under Section 6 means that every member of a group who agreed to commit an atrocity under this Act can be prosecuted and punished — even those who did not physically participate in the final act — significantly widening the net of accountability. This prevents dominant-caste groups from evading liability by delegating the actual commission of an atrocity to one person while others plan and support it.

definitions.definition: 'dependent' means the spouse, children, parents, brother and sister of the victim, who are dependent wholly or mainly on such victim for his support and maintenance.
definitions.plain_english: A 'dependent' is a close family member of the victim — specifically the victim's husband or wife, children, parents, or siblings — who relies on the victim for most or all of their financial support and daily needs. This relationship means if the victim is harmed, these family members also suffer because they depend on the victim economically. Only those family members who genuinely depend on the victim for their livelihood qualify under this definition.
real_world_examples: A Dalit agricultural labourer in rural Rajasthan is attacked in an atrocity and left unable to work. His wife and three minor children, who depend entirely on his daily wages for food and shelter, qualify as dependents and can claim relief, protection, and compensation under the Act.

An elderly Scheduled Tribe woman in Jharkhand is the sole breadwinner of her family. When she becomes a victim of an atrocity, her aged parents living with her and relying on her income for medicines and food are recognised as dependents entitled to notice of court proceedings under Section 15A.

A Scheduled Caste man in Tamil Nadu is murdered in a caste-based violence incident. His unmarried sister who lived with him and had no independent income, being financially maintained by him, is treated as a dependent and is entitled to be heard at bail and conviction proceedings.

A Scheduled Tribe youth in Odisha who financially supported his younger brother through school is a victim of an atrocity. The younger brother, having no other source of income, qualifies as a dependent and can apply to the Special Court to summon witnesses or documents relevant to the case.

A Scheduled Caste widow in Maharashtra runs a small business and supports her adult son who is disabled and unable to earn. When she is victimised under the Act, her disabled son is treated as a dependent entitled to social-economic rehabilitation and relocation support during trial.
what_it_covers: The spouse (husband or wife) of the victim who relies mainly or wholly on the victim for financial maintenance.
Minor or adult children of the victim who are financially supported by the victim and have no independent means of livelihood.
Parents of the victim who live with or are financially maintained by the victim and have no significant independent income.
A brother or sister of the victim who is wholly or mainly dependent on the victim for day-to-day support and maintenance.
A sibling with a disability or illness who cannot earn independently and depends on the victim for sustenance.
what_it_excludes: Extended family members such as aunts, uncles, grandparents, cousins, or in-laws, even if they live in the same household as the victim.
A spouse, child, sibling, or parent who is financially independent and does not rely on the victim for support and maintenance.
Individuals who are merely emotionally close to the victim but have no economic dependence on them for support.
Unmarried partners or live-in companions of the victim who are not legally recognised spouses.
Neighbours, community members, or friends of the victim, regardless of their social closeness or moral support role.
definitions.why_it_matters: Dependents are granted distinct legal rights under Section 15A, including the right to notice of court proceedings, the right to be heard at bail, discharge, conviction, and sentencing stages, and the right to apply to the Special Court or Exclusive Special Court to summon witnesses or documents — rights that cannot be exercised by any other person on behalf of the victim. Whether a person qualifies as a dependent directly determines their eligibility for State-provided protection, travelling and maintenance expenses, socio-economic rehabilitation, and relocation during investigation and trial under the Act.

definitions.definition: A devadasi is a woman belonging to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe who is dedicated to a deity, idol, object of worship, temple, or other religious institution through performance or promotion of such dedication or any other similar practice. The Act treats the act of performing, promoting, or permitting such dedication as a punishable atrocity under Section 3.
definitions.plain_english: A devadasi is a woman, typically from a lower-caste community, who is formally 'dedicated' or offered to a god, temple, or religious institution, often under the guise of religious custom. In practice, this system has historically meant such women are compelled into a life of servitude and sexual exploitation under the name of religion. The SC/ST Act makes it a criminal offence for anyone outside the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe community to perform, promote, or permit this practice against a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe woman.
real_world_examples: A dominant-caste village landlord in Karnataka pressures a Dalit family to dedicate their young daughter to the local goddess Yellamma, effectively enrolling her into the devadasi system against her will.

In a village in Andhra Pradesh, an upper-caste religious functionary performs a ritual tying a 'muttu' (sacred necklace) around a Scheduled Caste girl during a temple festival, formally dedicating her as a devadasi without the consent of the girl or her family.
A non-SC/ST temple trustee in Maharashtra actively organises and funds a ceremony in which a Dalit woman is dedicated to a local deity, promoting the devadasi practice in the community.

In Tamil Nadu, a non-SC/ST village headman permits and oversees a traditional 'pottukattu' ceremony where a young Scheduled Tribe woman is dedicated to a deity, knowing it will lead to her exploitation.

An upper-caste priest in Telangana encourages and facilitates a Scheduled Caste family, through religious pressure and social coercion, to dedicate their daughter to the temple as a devadasi, thereby committing an offence under Section 3 of the SC/ST Act.
what_it_covers: A Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe woman who is formally dedicated to a deity, idol, or temple through a religious ceremony.
Any woman subjected to a similar practice of dedication to a religious institution, even if not explicitly called 'devadasi', that results in religious servitude or exploitation.
Cases where dedication is performed, promoted, or permitted by a person who is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, making it a punishable atrocity.
Rituals, ceremonies, or acts — such as tying a sacred thread or necklace — that formally consecrate a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe woman to a religious entity.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary religious vows or service undertaken freely by a woman who is not a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member, which fall outside the SC/ST Act's scope entirely.

Acts of dedication performed by a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe community upon another member of the same community, as the SC/ST Act's penal provisions require the perpetrator to be a non-SC/ST person.
General religious service or employment at a temple (such as a priest or worker) where there is no element of forced dedication or exploitation linked to caste identity.
Historical or academic documentation, research, or cultural study of the devadasi system, which does not constitute 'performing or promoting' the practice under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: If an act qualifies as performing, promoting, or permitting the dedication of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe woman as a devadasi or similar practice under Section 3, the perpetrator (being a non-SC/ST person) commits a punishable atrocity under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, attracting imprisonment and fine, special court jurisdiction, and mandatory investigation protocols. This definition is critical because it determines whether the stringent protective machinery of the Act — including the presumption of guilt and special prosecution — is triggered.

An accused person who has been directed by the Special Court in Maharashtra to leave a taluka under section 10 returns to the same area within the prohibited period without written permission, leading to his arrest under section 11 and forcible removal in police custody.

A person subject to an externment order in Tamil Nadu applies to the Special Court for temporary permission to return to his village to attend a family function; the court grants a three-day conditional return with a surety bond, after which he must leave again.

A caste-based land encroacher in Uttar Pradesh against whom an externment order has been made refuses to allow police to photograph him as required under section 12, and is consequently prosecuted under section 186 of the Indian Penal Code for obstructing a public servant.

definitions.plain_english: A First Information Report (FIR) is the first formal written complaint recorded by the police when someone reports a crime. real_world_examples: A Dalit farmer in Rajasthan is forcibly dispossessed of his land by upper-caste neighbours; he approaches the local police station and the officer in charge is duty-bound to register an FIR under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, read it back to the complainant, and hand over a free copy immediately.

A Scheduled Tribe woman in Jharkhand reports being assaulted and humiliated on account of her caste identity; the Station House Officer must record the FIR, include relevant sections of the Act, and provide a photocopy to the victim at no charge the same day.

In Maharashtra, a Scheduled Caste youth's house is set on fire by a group of higher-caste individuals; when his family reports this to the police, the officer is required to register the FIR under appropriate provisions of the Atrocities Act and cannot refuse or delay registration.

A witness to an atrocity against a Dalit community in Tamil Nadu faces threats from the perpetrators; under Section 15A, the investigating officer must record any complaint of intimidation by the witness, and the witness is entitled to receive a photocopy of the FIR free of cost.

A public servant (police sub-inspector) in Uttar Pradesh deliberately refuses to register an FIR filed by a Scheduled Caste complainant alleging caste-based abuse; under Section 4, such wilful neglect of the duty to register the FIR makes the sub-inspector liable for imprisonment of not less than six months.

The document that must be read aloud to the informant before their signature is taken, and of which a free copy must be immediately furnished to the informant or victim.
FIRs registered under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act that form the basis for investigation, filing of charge sheets, and proceedings before the Special Court or Exclusive Special Court.

Internal administrative complaints or representations made to departmental authorities against a public servant, which do not constitute an FIR under this Act.
Anonymous complaints or tip-offs that have not been formally recorded, read back, and signed by an identified informant at a police station.
Private complaints filed under Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before a magistrate, which follow a different procedure from the FIR mechanism under this Act.

definitions.plain_english: Forest rights refer to the legally recognised rights of Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers to live in, use, and protect forest land and its resources, as defined under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. real_world_examples: A group of non-tribal contractors forcibly evicts an Adivasi family from their forest land in Jharkhand where they have been cultivating for generations, thereby violating their recognised forest rights under the Forest Rights Act — an offence punishable under the SC/ST Act.

In Chhattisgarh, a forest officer destroys the crop of a Scheduled Tribe farmer grown on pattas (title documents) issued under the Forest Rights Act, interfering with their forest rights and attracting liability under the SC/ST Act.

In Odisha, upper-caste landlords block a tribal village from accessing a community forest area used for collecting mahua flowers and tendu leaves, denying them their minor forest produce rights and constituting an atrocity under the SC/ST Act.

A revenue official in Madhya Pradesh fabricates land records to show that a Scheduled Tribe community's forest land is government property, dispossessing them of their forest rights — triggering prosecution under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

In Maharashtra's Gadchiroli district, a timber contractor intimidates a tribal gram sabha to prevent them from exercising their community forest resource management rights under the Forest Rights Act, which is treated as interference with forest rights under the SC/ST Act.

General land ownership or tenancy rights over non-forest land, which are covered by ordinary revenue or tenancy laws and do not fall within the scope of forest rights.

definitions.definition: Good faith, as used under this Act, refers to any act done or intended to be done honestly and without any fraudulent, malicious, or improper motive in the discharge of duties or exercise of powers under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. An act is deemed to be in good faith if it is performed with sincerity of purpose and reasonable care, even if it results in error or causes unintended harm.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely while carrying out responsibilities under this law, without any bad or harmful intentions. It protects government officials, authorities, and other persons from being sued or prosecuted when they genuinely try to do the right thing under this Act. Even if a mistake is made, if the person truly believed they were acting correctly and within the law, they are protected.
real_world_examples: A District Magistrate in Uttar Pradesh orders preventive detention of an accused person under the Act based on credible reports of imminent atrocity against a Dalit community — even if the order is later found procedurally deficient, the DM is protected if the action was taken honestly and without malice.

A police officer in Rajasthan registers a First Information Report and arrests a suspect based on prima facie evidence of an atrocity against a Scheduled Tribe member; if the prosecution fails due to insufficient evidence, the officer cannot be sued for wrongful arrest if the action was in good faith.

A State Government official in Tamil Nadu, acting under the Act, issues an externment order to remove a habitual offender who threatens Scheduled Caste residents; even if the order is later challenged and set aside by a court, the official enjoys protection if the order was issued without corrupt or malicious intent.

A Special Public Prosecutor in Maharashtra, while conducting a prosecution under the Act, discloses certain witness details to facilitate legal proceedings; if this was done genuinely to further the case and not for personal gain or to harm the witness, the action qualifies as good faith and is legally protected.

A social welfare officer in Madhya Pradesh implements a rehabilitation scheme for victims of atrocities but inadvertently disburses funds to ineligible beneficiaries due to clerical error; since the action was taken honestly and without fraud, the officer is shielded from prosecution under Section 22.

what_it_excludes: Actions taken with corrupt, malicious, or fraudulent intent against a person, even if the officer claims to have acted under the Act — such acts do not qualify as good faith and are not protected.
Acts of deliberate negligence or wilful disregard of law by a public servant or authority, where the person knowingly violated procedural safeguards or ignored clear legal mandates.

definitions.plain_english: A manual scavenger is a person who is made to clean or carry human waste by hand, typically from dry toilets, open drains, or pits, without proper sanitation equipment. It includes land, dwelling premises, agricultural produce, and any other material holdings over which the victim holds rights or interests.
definitions.plain_english: Property here refers to anything a person owns or has rights over — like land, a house, crops, livestock, or other belongings. Under this law, if a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe member suffers damage or loss to their property because of a caste-based atrocity, they are recognised as a victim and entitled to legal protection and relief. The term covers both physical assets and legally recognised rights over resources.
real_world_examples: A Dalit farmer's standing wheat crop in Uttar Pradesh is deliberately set on fire by upper-caste individuals to intimidate and dispossess him — the destruction of his crop constitutes harm to his property under this Act.

A Scheduled Tribe family's hut and household belongings in Jharkhand are demolished by a non-tribal landlord seeking to illegally occupy their land — the damage to their dwelling premises amounts to harm to property triggering victim status.

An SC community's borewell and irrigation infrastructure in Rajasthan is vandalised by dominant-caste members to deny them water access — the destruction of irrigation facilities constitutes property harm under the Act.

A Dalit woman's jewellery and household goods in Tamil Nadu are seized and not returned by a dominant-caste employer as a form of economic coercion — the deprivation of her movable possessions qualifies as harm to property.

A Scheduled Tribe member's forest produce collected under recognised forest rights in Odisha is forcibly taken away by non-tribal traders — the loss of produce and forest rights-based assets constitutes property harm under this Act.

Dwelling houses, huts, or any premises occupied by a member of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.
Forest produce, irrigation facilities, water resources, and other assets over which a Scheduled Tribe member holds recognised forest rights.
Movable possessions such as livestock, tools, vehicles, and household goods belonging to SC/ST members.
Any intangible rights over property, such as legally recognised land entitlements or allotment orders, interference with which causes monetary or material harm.
what_it_excludes: Property belonging to persons who are not members of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, as the protective scope of the Act does not extend to such individuals under this provision.
Harm or loss to property arising from purely civil disputes, natural disasters, or causes unconnected to the commission of an offence under this Act.
Intellectual property or purely reputational interests, which are not within the material and possessory scope of property as contemplated in the Act's provisions.
Property rights of non-tribal or non-SC third parties claimed over land that overlaps with SC/ST holdings, which are not protected under this Act.
Speculative or future economic interests not yet materialised into actual assets or recognised rights at the time of the offence.

definitions.definition: A Public Prosecutor specified as a Special Public Prosecutor or an advocate referred to in section 15, appointed by the State Government by notification in the Official Gazette, who has been in practice as an advocate for not less than seven years, for the purpose of conducting cases in a Special Court or Exclusive Special Court established under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A Public Prosecutor under this Act is a government-appointed lawyer who represents the State in cases involving atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The State Government formally appoints this person either from existing Public Prosecutors or by selecting a lawyer with at least seven years of practice experience. Their main job is to argue cases on behalf of victims in the Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts set up under this law.
real_world_examples: The Maharashtra State Government issues a Gazette notification appointing an advocate with 10 years of practice as a Special Public Prosecutor to conduct SC/ST atrocity cases before the Special Court in Nagpur.

In a case where a Dalit farmer in Rajasthan is subjected to violence and land dispossession, the designated Special Public Prosecutor appears before the Special Court in Jaipur to present evidence and argue for conviction of the accused upper-caste landlords.

The Telangana Government specifies a senior Public Prosecutor already serving in the district courts as the Special Public Prosecutor for the Exclusive Special Court in Hyderabad, issuing the required Official Gazette notification.

A Special Public Prosecutor in Tamil Nadu informs the victim and her dependents about upcoming bail hearings in an SC/ST atrocity case as required under Section 15A, ensuring the victim's right to be heard is protected.

Following a mass atrocity against a Scheduled Tribe community in Jharkhand's forested region, the State Government urgently appoints an advocate with eight years of experience as Special Public Prosecutor through an emergency Gazette notification to handle the cluster of cases before the Exclusive Special Court.
what_it_covers: An existing Public Prosecutor already serving in the State legal system who is formally specified by the State Government via Official Gazette notification to conduct SC/ST atrocity cases in a Special Court.

A private advocate with a minimum of seven years of practice experience who is appointed by the State Government through an Official Gazette notification to serve as Special Public Prosecutor or Exclusive Special Public Prosecutor.
An Exclusive Special Public Prosecutor appointed exclusively to conduct cases before an Exclusive Special Court established under Section 14(1) of this Act.
Any advocate or prosecutor who, once appointed, carries duties under Section 15A such as informing victims about court proceedings including bail hearings.
what_it_excludes: An advocate with less than seven years of practice experience, who cannot be appointed as a Special Public Prosecutor under this Act regardless of other qualifications.

A Public Prosecutor or advocate who has not been formally specified or appointed by the State Government through a notification in the Official Gazette, as informal or verbal designations do not satisfy the statutory requirement.
Defence lawyers or advocates appointed by the accused, who represent the opposite side and do not fall within the scope of this role.
Legal aid counsel appointed to assist victims directly under Section 15A, whose role is distinct from that of the prosecuting Special Public Prosecutor representing the State.

definitions.definition: 'Public servant' means a public servant as defined under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), as well as any other person deemed to be a public servant under any other law for the time being in force, and includes any person acting in his official capacity under the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be.
definitions.plain_english: A public servant, under this Act, is anyone who holds a government job or performs official duties on behalf of the Central or State Government. This includes all categories of government employees listed in the Indian Penal Code, as well as anyone else treated as a public servant by any other law in India. The term is intentionally broad to cover virtually anyone exercising official governmental authority.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Rajasthan who refuses to register an FIR filed by a Dalit woman alleging assault by an upper-caste landlord, thereby failing his statutory duty, qualifies as a public servant whose neglect can be punished under this Act.

A District Collector in Uttar Pradesh who deliberately delays or denies the allotment of government land to a Scheduled Tribe beneficiary, acting in his official capacity, is a public servant liable under this Act.

A Block Development Officer in Maharashtra who refuses to disburse welfare scheme funds specifically sanctioned for Scheduled Caste families, acting in dereliction of official duty, constitutes a public servant under this provision.

A government schoolteacher in Tamil Nadu who, in his official capacity, forces a Dalit child to sit separately from other students or perform menial tasks degrading to the child's dignity, can be held accountable as a public servant under this Act.

An employee of a Public Sector Undertaking or government corporation who, while performing official functions, discriminates against or facilitates atrocities against a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe is covered as a public servant under this Act.

A judicial magistrate or court officer who, in their official capacity, deliberately delays or obstructs proceedings initiated under this Act against an accused committing atrocities against Scheduled Caste individuals, falls within the ambit of public servant for purposes of accountability.
what_it_covers: All categories of persons enumerated under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, including legislators, judges, army officers, police officers, government clerks, and jurors acting in official capacity.

Any person acting in an official capacity under the Central Government or a State Government, such as District Collectors, Tehsildars, Block Development Officers, police inspectors, and revenue officials.

Persons deemed to be public servants under other laws in force in India, such as employees of public sector banks under the Banking Regulation Act, employees of statutory corporations, and public university officials.
Government school teachers, medical officers at government hospitals, and officials of government-aided institutions who exercise official authority over members of the public.
Election officials, census officers, and other persons temporarily vested with governmental authority to perform specific public functions.

Employees of purely private companies or corporations with no government stake or statutory backing, even if they perform services that may be considered socially important.
Members of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) or charitable trusts, unless specifically vested with governmental functions or deemed public servants under a specific statute.
Elected members of gram panchayats or local bodies acting in a purely political or personal capacity, as opposed to exercising an official governmental function under statutory authority.
Contractual daily-wage workers engaged by a government department for non-official menial tasks who exercise no authority or discretion over members of the public.

definitions.definition: 'Scheduled Areas' means the areas referred to in article 244 of the Constitution of India, being areas declared as such by the President of India through a public notification, typically covering regions with significant tribal populations and governed by the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, within which special protections and restrictions under this Act apply.
definitions.plain_english: Scheduled Areas are specific geographic regions in India, officially declared by the President, that are home to large tribal communities and receive special constitutional protection. These areas are listed under the Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution and are found in states like Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan. Because tribal people in these areas are considered particularly vulnerable to exploitation and atrocities, special laws and safeguards apply there.
real_world_examples: A non-tribal landlord in a Fifth Schedule area in Jharkhand attempts to forcibly occupy tribal agricultural land belonging to an Adivasi farmer — the Special Court can invoke Section 10 to remove such a person from the Scheduled Area before the offence occurs.

In the Scheduled Areas of Odisha's Sundargarh district, a moneylender repeatedly harasses and threatens a Scheduled Tribe family; the Special Court, satisfied by a police report, directs the moneylender to leave the notified tribal belt for up to three years.

A contractor in the Scheduled Areas of Chhattisgarh who is likely to engage tribal workers in begar (forced labour) is served a removal order by the Special Court under Section 10, preventing him from entering the area.

In the Scheduled Areas of Madhya Pradesh's Bastar region, a group of persons identified as likely to enforce a social or economic boycott against Scheduled Tribe members is ordered to vacate the demarcated tribal area by the Special Court.

A real estate developer in the Fifth Schedule area of Gujarat's Dahod district, who is believed to be conspiring to fraudulently transfer tribal land, is directed by the Special Court to remove himself from those Scheduled Areas for a specified period.

definitions.plain_english: Tribal areas are specific geographic regions in India that are officially recognised under the Constitution as areas where tribal (Adivasi) communities live. real_world_examples: In Jharkhand, a landlord who repeatedly threatens Santhali tribal villagers over land in a Fifth Schedule notified tribal area can be ordered by the Special Court to leave that area for up to three years under Section 10.

In Chhattisgarh, a moneylender who coerces Gond tribal families into bonded labour arrangements in a notified tribal area can be externmed from that region on a complaint before the Special Court.

In Odisha, a non-tribal businessman encroaching on tribal forest lands in a Fifth Schedule area and threatening tribal farmers may be directed by the Special Court to move beyond the limits of the tribal area to prevent an imminent offence.

In Assam's Sixth Schedule autonomous district councils, a person repeatedly assaulting Bodo tribal members in a notified tribal area can face a removal order from the Special Court restricting re-entry for up to three years.

definitions.definition: As applied under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 'unlawful assembly' has the same meaning as assigned under section 141 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), by virtue of section 6 of this Act, which incorporates section 149 and related provisions of the IPC — meaning an assembly of five or more persons with a common object to commit any of the offences specified in section 141 IPC, including overawing government, resisting legal process, committing mischief, or compelling any person to do what he is not legally bound to do.
definitions.plain_english: An unlawful assembly is a group of five or more people who gather together with the shared illegal purpose of intimidating others, resisting law enforcement, or causing harm. Under the SC/ST Act, if such a group collectively commits or assists in committing atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, every member of that group can be held equally responsible. This means even those who did not personally act but were part of the group can be prosecuted.
real_world_examples: A group of ten upper-caste villagers in Rajasthan assembles outside a Dalit family's home with the shared intention of forcibly evicting them from land they legally own, shouting casteist slurs and threatening violence — this constitutes an unlawful assembly committing an atrocity.

In a village in Uttar Pradesh, more than five dominant-caste men gather at the entry of a Scheduled Tribe hamlet to enforce an economic boycott, blocking supplies and intimidating traders from selling to tribal residents — the entire group is liable under the SC/ST Act read with IPC section 149.

During a protest in Maharashtra, a mob of at least five persons assembles and forces a Dalit man to parade without clothes through the village street as an act of humiliation — each member of the assembly is equally culpable for the atrocity.

In Tamil Nadu, a group of six landlords assemble to intimidate an SC woman who filed a complaint of land encroachment against them, threatening her with harm if she does not withdraw the case — their collective assembly for this common illegal object makes all of them liable.

In Jharkhand, a group of seven non-tribal persons gather and forcibly occupy forest land held by a Scheduled Tribe community under the Forest Rights Act, dismantling boundary markers — the assembly with that common object attracts liability under the SC/ST Act for every participant.

definitions.definition: "Witness" means any person who is acquainted with the facts and circumstances, or is in possession of any information or has knowledge necessary for the purpose of investigation, inquiry or trial of any crime involving an offence under this Act, and who is or may be required to give information or make a statement or produce any document during investigation, inquiry or trial of such case and includes a victim of such offence.
definitions.plain_english: A witness is anyone who knows something relevant about a crime committed under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act — whether they saw it happen, heard about it, or have documents related to it. This includes people who may be asked to share information with the police, during an inquiry, or in court. Importantly, even the victim of the offence is treated as a witness under this law.
real_world_examples: A Dalit agricultural labourer in Rajasthan is assaulted by an upper-caste landlord. A neighbour who witnessed the assault and can identify the attacker qualifies as a witness under this Act.

In a village in Uttar Pradesh, a Scheduled Tribe woman is forced into bonded labour. The local village head who has knowledge of the arrangement and can testify about it is a witness, even if not directly involved.

A shopkeeper in Tamil Nadu who refused to sell goods to a Scheduled Caste family as part of an economic boycott is reported to police. A customer present at the time who saw the refusal and can give a statement to the investigating officer is a witness.

A Scheduled Caste government employee in Maharashtra files a complaint alleging humiliation by colleagues. A co-worker who heard the derogatory remarks and is asked to produce WhatsApp messages or give a statement before the Special Court qualifies as a witness.

In a case of manual scavenging in Gujarat, a municipal supervisor who has knowledge about which workers were assigned to clean sewers manually is summoned to produce records during the investigation and is therefore a witness.

The victim of an atrocity in Bihar — a Scheduled Tribe person whose land was forcibly grabbed — who testifies about the incident before the Exclusive Special Court is simultaneously the victim and a witness under this Act.

A person who has heard or received information about the offence indirectly but whose knowledge is considered necessary for the investigation or trial.
Any individual required to make a statement before the investigating officer under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in connection with an offence under this Act.
what_it_excludes: A person who has absolutely no knowledge, acquaintance with facts, or possession of information relevant to any offence under the Act — a completely uninvolved stranger.
Legal counsel or advocates representing parties in the case, who appear in their professional capacity and are not called to give factual testimony.
Judges, magistrates, or members of the Special Court or Exclusive Special Court who adjudicate the case, as they are not required to give information or statements in the proceedings.
A person whose only connection to the case is being mentioned in passing in documents without possessing any personal knowledge or information about the offence.

Expert witnesses in the narrow technical sense who are not acquainted with the facts of the specific case but only provide general opinion — unless they also possess relevant case-specific information.

definitions.definition: The term 'wrongfully' as used in Section 3 of the Act denotes an act done without legal right, authority, or justification, including occupation, cultivation, or dispossession of land belonging to or allotted to a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe that is contrary to law, against the person's will, without the person's consent, or with consent obtained through fear of death or hurt, or by fabricating records of such land.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongfully means doing something without any legal right or valid reason — especially taking over, farming, or throwing someone off their land when you have no legal permission to do so. It includes situations where someone is forced out against their will, tricked into giving permission, or where fake documents are used to grab the land. In simple terms, it means acting in an unlawful or unjust manner against a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe person's property rights.
real_world_examples: An upper-caste landlord in rural Rajasthan forcibly ploughs and sows crops on a Dalit family's government-allotted land without any court order or legal right, constituting wrongful occupation and cultivation under Section 3.

A dominant community member in a village in Madhya Pradesh presents forged pattas (land records) to the revenue department to claim ownership of land allotted to an Adivasi family under the Forest Rights Act, amounting to wrongful dispossession through fabricated records.

A group of individuals in Uttar Pradesh physically drives a Scheduled Caste family out of their ancestral agricultural land by threatening violence, without any legal eviction order, thereby wrongfully dispossessing them under the Act.

In Bihar, a local contractor occupies a pond and irrigation channel whose use rights are vested in a Scheduled Tribe community, preventing them from irrigating their fields, which constitutes wrongful interference with their enjoyment of water and irrigation rights.

A landowner in Tamil Nadu harvests standing crops from land legally allotted to a Dalit farmer and takes away the produce without any legal claim, constituting wrongful dispossession and interference with the produce of the land.

In Maharashtra, a non-tribal person pressures a Scheduled Tribe woman into signing a land transfer deed by threatening harm to her family, thereby obtaining consent under duress — rendering the occupation wrongful under the Act.
